instruction.what: Step 3.1, the elements of one subgroup (stage 4, C1; the end of the loop for the subgroup): what the evidence of the subgroup shows of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being. The input is the evidence observations of the subgroup by marker (`to_take_up`, the senses first, then the 2.1 findings and the older evidence), not the verses; the verses are kept for an occasional read-back. A finding is a building block, never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (that is stage 5).
read: Read the observations to take up, in order: the senses (1.1) and their enrichments (1.2) first, then the 2.1 findings (pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, double meanings), then the older evidence. The inner-being workings work more with the senses than with the surfaces, so findings rest on the senses first.

For each item a finding may use (`uses`): what is done and its mode (operation, with its chain), whether a refusal or a pursuit (polarity), what it is directed at (object), the outward act (enactment), the other party with the route (party), the circumstance, and what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives the working (role, the dimension). Never the meaning of the word (stage 1).

Read the older inner-being observations (`older_inner_being`) with them: each is considered first, accepted with a trace to evidence, restated where it says more than the evidence, consumed where a finding says the same, merged, or deleted where it cannot be made true.
Go back to a verse (`verses`) only where the evidence does not settle the question, and say why.
write: Fill `answer.findings`: each one observation, with a `key` unique in the answer, `kind` (of the item's kinds), `text`, `basis` (stated or read), `parts` with `item` (one of `uses`) and what the item needs (with `grounds`), and `nodes`: a `traced` node on each observation it rests on (from `to_take_up` or `may_rest_on_besides`) and an `occurrence` node, with its `role` chosen from the verse (characteristic, qualifier, object, relational target, enactment or standalone), on the occurrences those observations cover.
An occurrence outside the observations a finding rests on is allowed only with a `read_back` entry on the finding: {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_used`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.

`older`: answer, once, each older inner-being observation (`older_inner_being`) that has a node on an occurrence your findings name (RW-13; the record lists any it misses, and refuses an answer to one on no named occurrence: those are shown, not demanded, IB-05): keep (with nature inner_being: it stands, traced to evidence), restate, merge, consume (carriers ["this"] or ids, mapping), delete_neither, or defer (collection, nature, finding).
`existing`: answer every earlier reading (`earlier_readings`: inner being of an earlier grouping on these occurrences) with accept, modify, delete, merge or leave, and its reason.
The text says what the evidence shows of the element; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never states the behaviour as a whole.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordElements -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but lexical, layer-1, layer-2 and layer-3) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route). A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

to_take_up.text: The lexicon entries bear the grouping out: the codes with the largest counts are the verbs of thinking and supposing (G1380 to think, G3543 to think, G3633 and G5282 to suppose, G5274 to take up, suppose) and the verb to say, whose Qal sense in the lexicon includes saying in one's heart and so thinking (H0559, the largest code with 40 occurrences), with H2803J (think, imagine), H1819 (to imagine,

God's thoughts, and the contrast with man's: his thoughts toward his people are many and very deep, the nations do not know the Lord's thoughts, his thoughts are not man's and are as high above them as the heavens, and his thoughts are precious to the psalmist. The thoughts are the Lord's own purposes and mind. Verses: Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Psa 139:17, Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9, Mic 4:12.

Conceiving evil as if in a womb: wicked people conceive trouble, chaff and mischief and give birth to evil, stubble and iniquity. The same verb of conceiving is turned to what a person forms within and brings out in act. Verses: Job 15:35, Isa 33:11, Isa 59:4.

Conceiving a child: the woman becomes pregnant and bears, in the promises and announcements of a son, in the question of the barren, in the cleansed woman who will conceive, in the confession of the psalmist that his mother conceived him in sin, and in the sign of the virgin. The words are Hebrew and Greek verbs and nouns of pregnancy and seed, and the English 'conceive' is bodily. Verses: Num 5:2

'Opinion' in the phrase about not caring for anyone's opinion: the Greek verb is of looking, and the phrase is that Jesus does not look at the person's face, that is, does not weigh people by standing. It is regard for status, not a view held. Verses: Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14.

Opinion as a view that a person holds and declares: Elihu is afraid to declare his opinion and then insists on it, and the fool takes pleasure only in declaring what his heart holds. It is a person's own view, set against understanding. Verses: Job 32:6, Job 32:10, Job 32:17, Pro 18:2.
'Perhaps' as the captain's hope that the god may give a thought to them: the Hebrew particle of possibility, carrying no thinking of its own. Verses: Jon 1:6.
'With no thought of war' as turning back from war: the Hebrew verb is of returning, said of the trusting passers-by who are stripped. It is a turning back, not a thought. Verses: Mic 2:8.
'Well thought of' as a good report: the Greek noun is of testimony, the overseer must have a good report from outsiders. It is how others speak of him, not what he thinks. Verses: 1Ti 3:7.

Thinking as the way the mind works, its understanding or frame: the thinking of people who knew God becomes futile, the believers are to be mature and not children in their thinking, and they are to arm themselves with Christ's way of thinking. It is the mind's mode, with a measure of maturity or futility. Verses: Rom 1:21, 1Cor 14:20, 1Pe 4:1.

A question that asks for a hearer's view: 'what do you think?' is put to Simon, to the hearers, to the lawyer, to the chief priests and to those looking for Jesus. It asks the person to give a judgment he already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.

What seems right or best in someone's eyes: the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom of what appears good to a person, rendered think, think best or thought good. It is a person's own judgment of what is good or fitting. Verses: Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:4, Jer 40:5, 2Sa 3:19.

A thought quoted as inner speech: the Hebrew verb of saying introduces what a person says in himself, and the quoted sentence gives the thought; the Greek of Luk 12:17 does the same with the rich man's words to himself. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will follow, and the verse often shows it wrong. Verses: Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2

Planning or intending: the Assyrian's heart is set on destroying nations, the prophets intend to make the people forget the name, the Lord will do to his people what he planned for the nations, and the one who speaks against God intends to change times and laws. The verbs are of devising and purpose. Verses: Job 6:26, Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, Num 33:56, 1Sa 18:25.

Giving thought to something: calling to mind, reflecting on, attending to, taking thought for or turning the mind to what is named: the psalmist thinks on his ways and on the Lord's rules, the Lord takes thought for the poor, the prudent give thought to their steps, the believer is to think on what is excellent, Jerusalem took no thought of her end. The word is attention of the mind to a matter or

Reckoning something as so, judging or counting: Paul judges it necessary, a thing is counted unclean by the one who holds it so, God's raising of the dead is judged incredible in Act 26:8, Judah takes the covered woman for a prostitute, and Job 41:32 counts the deep as white-haired. The word is a judgment that counts or takes something as of a certain kind. Verses: Job 35:2, Job 41:32, 2Cor 12:6,

Being minded: the way a person is set in mind, to rate oneself soberly in Rom 12:3, to hold the same mind or another in Phili 3:15, and the child's mindedness given up in 1Cor 13:11. The Greek verb is of being of a mind or having an attitude. Verses: Rom 12:3, Phili 3:15, 1Cor 13:11.

Thoughts as purposes and devices: the intention of the heart in Gen 6:5, the schemes of the wicked, the thoughts the righteous and the wicked hold, the thoughts to be forsaken, and the wicked thoughts that lodge within. The word is of purpose, plan and device, and the verses place it in the heart. Verses: 1Ch 28:9, Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Job 21:27, Psa 10:4, Psa 56:5, Psa 94:11, Pro 12:5, Pro 15:26,

Thoughts as what arises and is held in the mind, known to God or others: they come out of the heart, are perceived by Jesus, are alarmed or answered, are known by the spirit of the person or by the Lord, are shaped by ease, and are led astray. The words are nouns of thought, reasoning and musing, in many Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek words, with the heart or the mind as their place. Verses: Deu 15:9,

Supposing, holding a belief or imagining something to be so: the belief is stated or put in question, often about oneself or about another, and the verse tests, corrects or reproves it. The hearers think the Gentiles' many words will be heard, that Jesus cannot appeal to his Father, that he came to give peace, that they are wise, stand, or are religious; in the Hebrew verses the speaker is told wh

The codes of God's thoughts are H4284 (thought, device; plan, purpose) and H7454 (purpose, aim, thought). The lexicon bears out thoughts as purposes, here the Lord's own, set against man's in Isa 55:8 and Isa 55:9 and unknown to the nations in Mic 4:12.

The code of conceiving evil is H2029 (to conceive, become pregnant, bear). The lexicon gives only the bodily sense; Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4 turn it to trouble and mischief formed within and brought out: the figure is the verses', not the lexicon's.

The codes of conceiving a child are H2029 (to conceive), H2030A (pregnant), H2232 (to sow; to be made pregnant), H3179 (to be hot, conceive), G4815 (to become pregnant, conceive), G2602 (foundation, with the seed in Heb 11:11) and G4690G (seed, offspring); G1722 (in) and G2192 (to have) make the Greek phrase of having in the womb. The lexicon bears out a bodily conceiving with no act of thought.

The code behind opinion in Mat 22:16 and Mar 12:14 is G0991 (to see, look at). The lexicon gives seeing; the phrase is not looking at a person's standing, so no view is held: the English opinion is not the code's sense.

The codes of a declared opinion are H1843 (knowledge, opinion; judgment) in Job 32:6, Job 32:10 and Job 32:17 and H3820A (inner man, mind, heart) in Pro 18:2, where the fool's opinion is what is in his heart. The lexicon bears out a view held and spoken.
The code of thought in Jon 1:6 is H0194 (perhaps, peradventure). The lexicon gives a particle of possibility; it carries no thinking, and the giving of thought is the captain's hope about the god.
The code of with no thought of war in Mic 2:8 is H7725G (to return, turn back). The lexicon gives returning; the English thought is not in the code.
The code of well thought of in 1Ti 3:7 is G3141 (testimony; good reputation). The lexicon bears out a good report from others, not a thought of the overseer.

The codes of thinking as the mind's mode are G1261 (reasoning, thought) in Rom 1:21, G5424 (thinking, understanding) in 1Cor 14:20 and G1771 (attitude, thought, intention) in 1Pe 4:1. G2532 (and) is a connective in the unit. The lexicon bears out the mind's way of working, with futility or maturity named by the verses.

The code of what do you think is G1380 (to think, consider, regard; an action of the mind and heart for processing information into understanding and choices). The lexicon bears out asking for a judgment the hearer forms, in Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36 and Joh 11:56.

The code of what seems best is H5869I (eye; as showing mental qualities), with H0413 (to, toward). The lexicon bears out the eye as the seat of judgment in the idiom good in your eyes, in Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:4, Jer 40:5 and 2Sa 3:19.

The codes of a thought quoted as inner speech are H0559 (to say; to say in one's heart, to think, to intend), G1260 (to reason, deliberate) and G3004G (to say). H0834A (which), H0853 (the object marker) and H3588A (that, for) are small words in the units. The lexicon bears out saying in one's heart as the form of the thought, as in 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 18:11, 1Sa 18:17 and 1Sa 20:3.

The codes of planning or intending are H2803I (to plan, devise, mean), H2803J (to think, plan), H1819 (to imagine, think) and H5452 (to think, intend). The lexicon bears out devising and purpose, in Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, Num 33:56, 1Sa 18:25 and Job 6:26.

The codes of giving thought are H2803I and H2803J (to think, account), H2142 (to remember, call to mind), H0995 (to discern, consider), H1819 (to imagine, think), H6245B (to think), G3049 (to count, consider), G3421 (to remember, fix the thoughts upon), G3539 (to understand, reflect), G1760 (to reflect on) and G1761 (reflection). H1931 (he) is a pronoun in a unit. The lexicon bears out attention o

The codes of reckoning something as so are G3049 (to credit, count, reckon), G2233 (to think, consider, count), G2919 (to decide, consider) and H2803J (to think, account). G1161 (but) is a connective in a unit. The lexicon bears out a judgment that counts a thing as of a kind, in Rom 14:14, Gen 38:15, Act 26:8 and the others.
The code of being minded is G5426 (to think, regard, hold an opinion; to set one's mind on; to have a certain attitude). The lexicon bears out a set of mind, in Rom 12:3, Phili 3:15 and 1Cor 13:11.

The codes of thoughts as purposes are H4284 (thought, device; plan, purpose), H4209 (purpose, device, plot) and H1902H (meditation, plotting). The lexicon bears out purpose and device, placed by the verses in the heart, as in Gen 6:5 and 1Ch 28:9.

The codes of thoughts that arise and are held are G1261 (reasoning, thought), G1270 (thought), G1271 (mind, thinking), G1761 (reflection), G3540 (mind, thought; scheme, design), H4093 (knowledge, thought; place of knowledge), H5587B (disquietings), H6248 (thought, idea), H7454 (purpose, thought), H7476 (thought), H7808 (thought), H8312 (disquieting thoughts) and H2808 (reasoning). The codes of supposing something to be so are G1380 (to think, imagine, suppose, presume), G3543 (to suppose, presume, expect), G3633 (to think, suppose, presume), H0559 (to say in one's heart, to think), H1819 (to imagine, think) and H7200H (to see, consider). The lexicon bears out a belief held, which the verses test, as in 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12 and 1Cor 14:37.

Desire words stand with the group in 1Sa 18:25, 1Ch 28:9 and Jam 4:5: 'desires' 12 words before in 1Sa 18:25, 'willing' 9 before in 1Ch 28:9, 'yearns' 5 after in Jam 4:5. The surface 'will' of 2Sa 14:17 (4 after) and 2Ki 7:12 (13 before) is the particle and verb of the quoted speech, not a desire.

Heart or mind stands with the group in all ten verses. It is within three words of the member in Deu 15:9 and 2Sa 13:33 (1), Isa 10:7 (2), Eze 20:32 and Rom 1:21 (3); at 4 in 1Ch 28:9 (hearts), Mat 9:4 and 1Ti 6:5; at 6 in Eze 11:5; and at 10 in Jam 1:26 and 1Ch 28:9 (heart). The verses name the heart or mind as the place of the thought.

Intending stands with the group in 1Ch 28:9, Psa 64:5, Isa 10:7, Joh 11:13, Act 27:13 and Jam 4:5. The partner words are of the same kind as the member in 1Ch 28:9 (plan, 1 before), Psa 64:5 (purpose, 4 before) and Isa 10:7 (intend, 4 before); in Joh 11:13 'meant' is 2 after and is what Jesus meant, which they supposed otherwise; in Act 27:13 and Jam 4:5 'purpose' is 2 and 1 after.

The divine are God (31), the Lord (21), Jesus (8), Christ (5), the Most High and the possessive forms. In most the supposer is a named person who holds a view about another person or a state of affairs: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Saul, David, Naaman and Hezekiah hold a quoted thought, with the human entity before the member in 72 of 118 human pairs. The surface conceive carries codes of bodily conceiving in Num 5:28, Num 11:12, Judg 13:3, Judg 13:5, Judg 13:7, Psa 51:5, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23, Luk 1:31 and Heb 11:11: H2232, H2029, H2030A, H3179, G4815, and the Greek phrases of G1722 with G2192 and of G2602 with G4690G. Each is a woman becoming pregnant or a person conceived, with no act of thought.

In Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4 the same code H2029 is turned to what a person forms within: trouble, chaff and mischief are conceived and evil, stubble and iniquity are born. The figure of the womb is the verses' way of naming a thought formed and brought out in act.

The surface opinion carries H1843 in Job 32:6, Job 32:10 and Job 32:17, knowledge or a judgment that Elihu holds back and then declares, and H3820A in Pro 18:2, the heart, where the fool's opinion is what his heart holds. In these four it is a view a person holds and speaks.
In Mat 22:16 and Mar 12:14 opinion carries G0991, to see or look at: Jesus does not look at a person's standing. No view is held; the English word renders a phrase of not regarding the face.

In Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:4 and Jer 40:5 think carries H5869I, the eye, or H0413 with it, in the idiom of what is good in someone's eyes: the think is a person's own judgment of what is best or fitting.

In 2Ki 18:20, Isa 36:5, 2Ch 13:8 and Eze 11:5 think carries H0559, to say, in its sense of saying in one's heart: the thought is a view put into words, and in Eze 11:5 the Lord states what the house of Israel thinks.

Think carries the Hebrew and Aramaic verbs of reckoning and devising: H2803J in Job 6:26, Job 35:2, Job 41:32, Psa 119:59, Psa 144:3 and Jer 23:27, H2803I in Isa 10:7, H1819 in Est 4:13 and H5452 in Dan 7:25. In some the thought is a judgment held, in others a plan pursued.
In 2Sa 18:27 think carries H7200H, to see or consider: the watchman judges from what he sees. In Psa 119:52 it carries H2142, to remember: thinking of the rules from of old is calling them to mind.

Think carries G1380, to think or consider, in most of the Gospel verses and in 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23, 2Cor 11:16 and Heb 10:29: a view held about what is so, often asked of the hearer (Mat 17:25, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36) or corrected (Mat 26:53, Luk 12:51, Luk 13:2, Joh 5:45).

Think carries G3543, to suppose or deem, in Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Act 17:29 and 1Cor 7:26: in the first three the view is forbidden (do not think, we ought not to think), in 1Cor 7:26 Paul gives his own judgment.

Think carries G1760, to reflect, in Mat 9:4, G3539, to understand or perceive, in Eph 3:20, and G3049, to count or consider, in 2Cor 12:6 and Phili 4:8: the mind turned to a matter, evil in the heart in Mat 9:4 and what is excellent in Phili 4:8.

In Rom 12:3 and Phili 3:15 think carries G5426, to be minded, twice in each verse: a set of mind, sober rating of oneself, maturity. In 2Pe 1:13 it carries G2233, to consider, with G1161, a connective.

In Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9 and Psa 64:5 thinking carries H0559, to say, and the quoted sentence that follows gives the thought as inner speech: Jacob's plan for the camps, David's fear of report, Achish's trust, the enemies' hope that the work will stop. In Neh 6:9 H0853 is the object marker in the unit.

In Rom 1:21, 1Cor 14:20 and 1Pe 4:1 thinking is the mind's way of working: G1261 reasoning that became futile (with G2532, and), G5424 understanding to be mature and not childish, G1771 the attitude to arm oneself with.
In 2Cor 12:19 thinking carries G1380, a view held all along, in Phili 1:17 G3633, an intent to afflict, and in Heb 11:15 G3421, being mindful of the land they left.

The surface thinks carries H0559 in 1Sa 20:3, Saul's inner speech that David quotes, and in the New Testament G1380 in Luk 8:18, 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4 and Jam 1:26, G3049 in Rom 14:14 and G3543 in 1Cor 7:36. In most of the Greek verses it is a view of oneself that the verse tests: wise, standing, a prophet, something, religious.

In the narratives and sayings of Gen 20:11, Gen 26:9, Gen 31:31, Gen 32:20, Exo 2:14, Jos 22:28, Judg 3:24, Judg 15:2, Rut 4:4, 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 18:11, 1Sa 18:17, 1Sa 18:21, 1Sa 20:26, 2Sa 14:15, 2Sa 14:17, 2Sa 21:16, 2Ki 5:11, 2Ki 20:19, Job 29:18, Psa 94:18, Isa 39:8, Jer 3:7, Jer 3:19 and Eze 20:32 thought carries H0559, to say, and the thought is given as the quoted words a person said within. Thought carries Hebrew verbs of reckoning, devising, likening, remembering and discerning: H2803J in Gen 38:15 and Psa 73:16, H2803I in 1Sa 18:25 and Psa 40:17, H1819 in Num 33:56, Psa 48:9 and Psa 50:21, H5869I in 2Sa 3:19, H2142 in Lam 1:9, H0995 in Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29 (with H1931). The thought is a judgment, a plan, a likening or attention given.

Thought as a noun of what the mind holds: H1697G with H1961 in Deu 15:9 (an unworthy word in the heart), H4284 in 1Ch 28:9 (every plan and thought the Lord understands), H6248 in Job 12:5, H2808 in Ecc 9:10, H7808 in Amo 4:13. In Jon 1:6 H6245B is the god giving a thought, with H0194 perhaps; in Mic 2:8 H7725G is turning back, not a thought.

In the Gospels and Acts thought carries G1380 (Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29, Act 12:9), G3543 (Mat 20:10, Act 8:20) and G2919 (Act 26:8): a view taken of what is so, which the verse shows mistaken or in question. In Luk 12:17 it carries G1260 with G3004G, the rich man reasoning to himself.

In 1Cor 13:11 thought carries G5426, the child's mindedness; in 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25 G2233, a judgment of what is necessary; in 2Cor 10:5 G3540, every thought taken captive; in 1Ti 3:7 G3141, a good report from outsiders, not a thought.

In Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9 and Mic 4:12 thoughts carries H4284, purposes and plans, and in Psa 139:17 H7454: here the thoughts are the Lord's own, many, deep, precious, higher than man's and unknown to the nations.

In Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Psa 94:11, Pro 12:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7, Isa 66:18 and Jer 4:14 thoughts carries H4284, purposes and devices of people, most of them evil and known to the Lord; in Psa 10:4 H4209, the wicked man's purposes, and in Lam 3:62 H1902H, the musing of the assailants.

Thoughts carries H5587B, disquietings, in Job 20:2, H7454 in Psa 139:2, H8312, anxious thoughts, in Psa 139:23, H4093, the place of knowledge, in Ecc 10:20, and H1697I, things, in Eze 38:10: what rises and is held within, known to God.
In Dan 2:29, Dan 2:30, Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10 and Dan 7:28 thoughts carries the Aramaic H7476: thoughts that come in the night or alarm the one who has them.

In the New Testament thoughts carries G1761 in Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25 and Heb 4:12, G1261 in Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, 1Cor 3:20 and Jam 2:4, G1270 in Luk 11:17, G1271 in Luk 1:51, G3540 in 2Cor 11:3, and G3588, the article, in 1Cor 2:11: reasonings and designs of the heart, known by Jesus, by the Lord and by a person's own spirit.

A negator reaches the thinking itself in Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45, Act 17:29, Rom 12:3, 2Cor 11:16, Isa 10:7 and Lam 1:9: do not think, we ought not to think, let no one think, his heart does not so think, she took no thought. The view is forbidden or denied.

In Jos 22:28, 1Sa 20:26, 2Sa 5:6, Psa 10:4, Isa 55:8, Mic 4:12, Mat 6:7, Mat 22:16, Luk 12:51, Act 12:9, Rom 1:21, Jam 1:26 and the other verses of this group the negator stands in the quoted thought, in the content supposed, or on another verb of the sentence (know, honor, bridle, care, heap up, delay): it does not reach the thinking. Adjacency is not scope.

In Neh 6:9 the enemies think the workers' hands will drop from the work, and Nehemiah asks God to strengthen his hands: the prayer answers the enemies' thought.

In Mat 6:7 the Gentiles pray thinking many words will be heard: a false thought about prayer. In Mat 26:53 Jesus asks whether they think he cannot appeal to his Father: the thought misjudges his power to ask. In 2Sa 14:15 the woman thought the king might grant her request.

In Rom 1:21 those who knew God did not give thanks, and they became futile in their thinking: withholding thanks goes with the thinking becoming futile.
In Psa 139:23 the psalmist asks God to try him and know his thoughts: the thoughts are what the trying lays open.

In Lam 1:9 Jerusalem took no thought of her future and now cries out in affliction: the affliction follows the lack of thought. In Phili 1:17 some think to afflict Paul in prison: the thought aims at affliction. In 1Cor 7:26 Paul judges in view of the present distress, and in Job 15:35 trouble is conceived.

In 1Sa 27:12 Achish trusted David, thinking David had made himself hated by Israel: the trust rests on a mistaken thought. In 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 the Rabshakeh asks in whom they trust and whether they think words are strength for war. In Isa 59:4 they rely on empty pleas while they conceive mischief, and in Mic 2:8 the passers-by go trustingly.
In Psa 119:59 the psalmist thinks on his ways and turns his feet to the testimonies: the thinking leads the turning. In Jer 3:19 the Lord thought Israel would not turn from following him.

In Num 5:28 and Judg 13:7 clean and unclean go with conceive in its bodily sense.
In Pro 21:29 the upright gives thought to his ways, set against the wicked who puts on a bold face: the upright is marked by considering his way.
In Judg 15:2 the father thought Samson utterly hated her, and in 1Sa 27:12 Achish thought David an utter stench to Israel: utter marks how fully the mistaken thought judges.

In Psa 73:16 the psalmist's thinking how to understand wearies him.

may_rest_on_besides.text: The Greek is the idiom of having in the womb: the woman will be with child. It is bodily conception, said of the virgin in the quoted prophecy. Verses: Mat 1:23.

The Greek noun is the laying down of seed; with the next word it makes the phrase the English renders as the power to conceive, said of Sarah past the age. It names the act of conceiving, not a thought. Verses: Heb 11:11.
The Greek noun is seed, the word that completes the phrase rendered the power to conceive in this verse; the English folds the pair into one verb. Verses: Heb 11:11.
The Greek verb is to take together and so to conceive in the womb; the angel tells Mary she will conceive and bear a son. It is bodily conception. Verses: Luk 1:31.
In these two verses the Hebrew verb is bodily conception: Moses asks whether he conceived the people, and the angel tells the barren woman she will conceive. Verses: Num 11:12, Judg 13:3.

In these three verses the same verb is used figuratively: wicked people conceive trouble, chaff and mischief and give birth to evil, iniquity and stubble. The picture of pregnancy carries what is formed in a person and then brought out in act. Verses: Job 15:35, Isa 33:11, Isa 59:4.
The Hebrew verb is bodily conception, the angel's announcement of a son and the sign of the virgin; it is a promise of birth, not a thought. Verses: Judg 13:5, Judg 13:7, Isa 7:14.
The Hebrew verb is to be sown with seed: the woman cleared of defilement will be able to conceive children. It is bodily conception. Verses: Num 5:28.
The Hebrew verb is the warming that conceives: the psalmist says his mother conceived him in sin. It is bodily conception, with sin placed at its start. Verses: Psa 51:5.

In these two verses the Greek is a verb of looking; the phrase is that Jesus does not look at the face of men, which the English renders as caring for no one's opinion. It names regard for other people's standing, not a view of his own. Verses: Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14.
In Job 32 'opinion' is Elihu's own view or knowledge, which he is afraid at first to declare because of his youth and then insists on declaring. Verses: Job 32:6, Job 32:10, Job 32:17.
In Pro 18:2 the Hebrew is the word for heart, the fool's own mind: he takes pleasure only in revealing what his heart holds, which the English renders as his opinion. Verses: Pro 18:2.
In Rom 1:21 'thinking' is the reasonings of the mind, the plural inner deliberation that became futile when people knew God and did not honor him. Verses: Rom 1:21.
In 2Cor 12:19 'thinking' is the readers assuming something, that Paul has been defending himself to them; the verse corrects it. Verses: 2Cor 12:19.
In 1Pe 4:1 'way of thinking' is the intent or mind-set believers are to arm themselves with, set beside Christ's suffering. Verses: 1Pe 4:1.
In Rom 1:21 this code is the Greek conjunction in the clause about becoming futile in thinking; it joins clauses and carries no thinking, which G1261 carries. Verses: Rom 1:21.
In Heb 11:15 'thinking of' is keeping in mind or remembering the land they left; the verse says that if they had kept it in mind they could have returned. Verses: Heb 11:15.
In Phili 1:17 'thinking' is supposing or intending: some preach out of ambition, expecting to add affliction to Paul in prison. Verses: Phili 1:17.
In 1Cor 14:20 'thinking' is the mind or understanding, the Greek noun for the seat of understanding; believers are not to be children in it, but mature. Verses: 1Cor 14:20.

In these eight verses the Hebrew verb of saying introduces a thought quoted as a sentence: Jacob, David, Achish, the Jebusites, the king of Israel, Sennacherib, Nehemiah's enemies and the wicked each 'say' it in themselves. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will not be seen. Verses: Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9, Psa 64:5.

In these seven verses 'thinks' is holding an estimate of oneself, that one has something, is wise, stands, is a prophet, is something, has confidence in the flesh, or is religious. Each time the verse tests the estimate and finds it wanting or sets another beside it. Verses: Luk 8:18, 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4, Jam 1:26.
In Rom 14:14 'thinks it unclean' is the reckoning of the person: the thing is unclean for the one who counts it so, though nothing is unclean in itself. Verses: Rom 14:14.
In 1Cor 7:36 'thinks' is judging his own conduct toward his betrothed to be improper; the Greek is a verb of holding as so, and the judgment is the man's own. Verses: 1Cor 7:36.
In 1Sa 20:3 'thinks' is the Hebrew verb of saying, quoting what Saul says in himself: that Jonathan must not know. It is inner speech about another person. Verses: 1Sa 20:3.
In 2Pe 1:13 this code is the Greek conjunction in the clause 'I think it right'; it carries no thinking, which the verb of G2233 carries. Verses: 2Pe 1:13.

In these seven verses 'think' is a question put to a hearer for his view: 'What do you think?' asks Jesus, and the hearers are asked about a case, a person or a coming. It asks for a judgment the hearer already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.

In these verses 'think' is holding a belief, often one the verse then corrects: the Gentiles' belief that many words are heard, the belief that Jesus cannot appeal to his Father, that he came to give peace, that the Galileans were worse, that the Scriptures give life apart from him, that killing believers serves God. In the Pauline verses it is Paul's own estimate of the apostles' place, of his ju
In Mat 9:4 'think evil' is to turn something over in the mind: Jesus asks why they entertain evil in their hearts, and the verse names the heart as the place. Verses: Mat 9:4.
In 2Pe 1:13 'I think it right' is judging or counting it fitting: Peter counts it right to remind them while he lives. Verses: 2Pe 1:13.
In 2Cor 12:6 'think more of me' is the estimate others form: Paul holds back lest anyone credit him with more than they see or hear. Verses: 2Cor 12:6.
In Phili 4:8 'think about these things' is a command to direct the mind to what is true, honorable and excellent: to reckon with them and dwell on them. Verses: Phili 4:8.
In Eph 3:20 'think' is to take in with the mind, to conceive: God does more than all that we ask or conceive, set beside asking. Verses: Eph 3:20.

In these verses 'think' is to hold something as so: Jesus tells the hearers not to suppose he came to abolish the law or bring peace, Paul says God is not to be thought like an image, and Paul gives his own judgment on remaining as one is. In the first three the held notion is a wrong one the verse corrects; in 1Cor 7:26 it is a considered view. Verses: Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Act 17:29, 1Cor 7:26.

In Rom 12:3 and Phili 3:15 'think' is the mind-set, the way one is minded: not to rate oneself above what is right but to be sober, and to hold the same mind or another. The verb names the direction of the mind, with a measure given. Verses: Rom 12:3, Phili 3:15.

In these four verses the Hebrew verb of saying is rendered 'think': the Assyrian asks whether words are strategy, Abijah accuses Jeroboam and Israel of thinking to withstand the Lord, and the Spirit says so the house of Israel thinks. It is the inner or said claim of those addressed. Verses: 2Ki 18:20, 2Ch 13:8, Isa 36:5, Eze 11:5.
In Est 4:13 'think' is the Hebrew verb of imagining or supposing: Mordecai warns Esther not to imagine to herself that she alone will escape. Verses: Est 4:13.
In Psa 119:52 'think of' is to call to mind: the psalmist recalls the Lord's rules from of old and takes comfort. Verses: Psa 119:52.

In Isa 10:7 'think' is the Hebrew verb of planning and devising: the Assyrian's heart is not set on the plan the Lord has, for his own purpose is destruction of nations; the verb is of planning. Verses: Isa 10:7.

In these three verses 'think' is reckoning or counting: whether one holds a thing just, whether one would reckon the deep to be white-haired, and the Lord taking account of the son of man. Verses: Job 35:2, Job 41:32, Psa 144:3.
In Job 6:26 and Jer 23:27 'think' is to plan or intend: Job asks whether his friends intend to reprove words, and the prophets intend to make the people forget the name. Verses: Job 6:26, Jer 23:27.
In Psa 119:59 'think' is to reflect: the psalmist considers his ways and turns his feet to the testimonies; the reflection leads to action. Verses: Psa 119:59.
In Dan 7:25 'think' is the Aramaic verb of intending: the one who speaks against the Most High means to change the times and the law. Verses: Dan 7:25.

In these four verses 'think' renders the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom 'in the eyes of': what seems right or best to someone. It is how a person sees or judges a matter. Verses: Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:5.
In 2Sa 18:27 'I think' is the watchman's judgment from what he sees: the running of the first is like that of Ahimaaz. It is an impression from sight. Verses: 2Sa 18:27.

In these seven verses 'thoughts' are the reasonings of the mind, which come out of the heart, are known or perceived by Jesus, are revealed from many hearts, are futile for the wise, and become evil in the judge. They are inner reasonings with the heart as their place and Jesus as their knower. Verses: Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, 1Cor 3:20, Jam 2:4.
In Luk 11:17 'thoughts' is the inner thinking of the hearers that Jesus knows before he answers. Verses: Luk 11:17.
In Luk 1:51 'thoughts' is the mind or understanding of the proud, scattered by the Lord's arm. Verses: Luk 1:51.

In Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25 and Heb 4:12 'thoughts' is inner reflection that Jesus knows and that the word of God discerns; the two Matthew verses have Jesus answer them, and Hebrews names them with the intentions of the heart. Verses: Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Heb 4:12.
In 2Cor 11:3 'thoughts' are the mind's products or schemes, which Paul fears will be led astray from devotion to Christ as Eve was. Verses: 2Cor 11:3.

In 1Cor 2:11 this code is the Greek article in 'the things of a person', which the English renders as a person's thoughts; the verse says only the person's spirit knows them, as only God's Spirit knows God's. Verses: 1Cor 2:11.

In Eze 38:10 'thoughts' is the Hebrew word for words or matters that come up, here the matters that rise in the mind of Gog before he devises a scheme: something arises, then the person works on it. Verses: Eze 38:10.
In Lam 3:62 'thoughts' is the murmuring of the assailants, the Hebrew word for what is muttered or devised, set with their lips against the speaker all day. Verses: Lam 3:62.
In Ecc 10:20 'thoughts' is the mind or knowledge within, where a person might curse the king; the verse warns that even there it may be carried. Verses: Ecc 10:20.
In Psa 10:4 'thoughts' are the wicked man's schemes or devices, summed up as that there is no God. Verses: Psa 10:4.

In these verses 'thoughts' are the purposes and devisings of people: the intention of the heart in Gen 6:5, purposes kept in the heart in 1Ch 29:18, schemes against others, the just thoughts of the righteous and the foul ones of the wicked, the thoughts to be forsaken, thoughts of iniquity, the thoughts God knows and wicked thoughts that lodge within. Verses: Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Job 21:27, Psa 56:
In Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5 and Mic 4:12 'thoughts' are the Lord's: his thoughts toward his people, very deep, and a plan that the nations do not know. Verses: Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Mic 4:12.
In Isa 55:8 and Isa 55:9 the same word sets God's thoughts against man's: his are not ours and are as high above ours as heaven is above the earth. Verses: Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9.
In Job 20:2 'thoughts' are the disquieting thoughts that press on Zophar and answer him from within, because of his haste. Verses: Job 20:2.
In Psa 139:2 and Psa 139:17 'thoughts' are what the mind holds: the psalmist's thought is known to God from afar, and God's thoughts are precious and vast to him. Verses: Psa 139:2, Psa 139:17.

In these Aramaic verses 'thoughts' are the thoughts that rise in the mind: in Dan 2:29 thoughts come in bed about what will be, and in the other verses the king's and Daniel's thoughts alarm them. The same thoughts carry revelation in one place and fear in the others. Verses: Dan 2:29, Dan 2:30, Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10, Dan 7:28.
In Psa 139:23 'thoughts' are the anxious thoughts that the psalmist asks God to search and know, with the heart named beside them. Verses: Psa 139:23.
In Luk 12:17 'thought' is reasoning within oneself: the rich man deliberates in himself what to do about his crops. Verses: Luk 12:17.

In these five verses 'thought' is supposing something to be so: the disciples take Jesus for a ghost, the others take him for a spirit, the disciples take his word of sleep as rest, some take Judas's errand as a purchase, and Peter takes the angel's act for a vision. In each case the supposition is wrong. Verses: Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29, Act 12:9.
In 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25 'thought it necessary' is judging or counting it needful: Paul decides on the sending he describes. Verses: 2Cor 9:5, Phili 2:25.
In Act 26:8 'thought' is judged: Paul asks why it is judged incredible by the hearers that God raises the dead. Verses: Act 26:8.
In Luk 12:17 the Greek is the verb of saying; the English 'he thought to himself' renders it as what the man said in himself. It is inner speech. Verses: Luk 12:17.

In 1Ti 3:7 'well thought of' is the Greek noun for testimony or good report: the overseer is to have a good report from those outside. It is how others speak of him, not what he thinks. Verses: 1Ti 3:7.
In 2Cor 10:5 'thought' is the mind's product: Paul takes every thought captive to obey Christ, set beside arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. Verses: 2Cor 10:5.

In Mat 20:10 and Act 8:20 'thought' is an assumption of the person: the workers hired first expect more, and Simon assumes the gift of God can be bought. In both the verse shows the assumption to be wrong. Verses: Mat 20:10, Act 8:20.
In 1Cor 13:11 'thought' is how the child was minded; the verse sets it with speaking and reasoning as childish ways given up in adulthood. Verses: 1Cor 13:11.
In Jon 1:6 this code is the Hebrew particle 'perhaps' in the captain's hope that the god may give a thought to them; it carries a possibility, with no thinking of its own. Verses: Jon 1:6.

In these twenty-five verses 'thought' is the Hebrew verb of saying, quoting what a person says in himself: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the servants, Saul, the woman of Tekoa, Naaman, Hezekiah, the psalmist and others each state in a quoted sentence what they judged or expected, and the verse usually shows the thought wrong or about to be tested. It is inner speech about what will happen or what

In Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29 'gives thought to his steps' is attending carefully to one's way: the prudent and the upright consider where they go, set against the simple and the wicked. Verses: Pro 14:15, Pro 21:29.
In Deu 15:9 'thought' is the Hebrew word for a matter or word that arises in the heart, here an unworthy one against lending near the year of release. Verses: Deu 15:9.
In Num 33:56 'thought to do' is the Lord's own intention toward the peoples of the land: if Israel fails to drive them out, what he planned for those peoples he will do to Israel. Verses: Num 33:56.
In Psa 48:9 'thought on' is meditating on the Lord's steadfast love in the temple; the Hebrew is to dwell on something with the mind. Verses: Psa 48:9.
In Psa 50:21 'thought' is the false likeness the wicked imagine: that God is one like themselves. The Hebrew is of likening, and it is rebuked. Verses: Psa 50:21.
In Deu 15:9 this code is the Hebrew verb 'to be' in the clause 'lest there be an unworthy thought'; it carries no thinking, which the noun of H1697 carries. Verses: Deu 15:9.
In Lam 1:9 'took no thought' is the Hebrew verb of remembering: Jerusalem did not remember or consider her end. Verses: Lam 1:9.

In 1Sa 18:25 and Psa 40:17 'thought' is the Hebrew verb of devising and taking thought: Saul plans an end for David, and the Lord takes thought for the poor psalmist. In the first it is a plan against a person; in the second care for one. Verses: 1Sa 18:25, Psa 40:17.
In Gen 38:15 'thought' is reckoning or taking someone for something: Judah takes the veiled woman for a prostitute. Verses: Gen 38:15.
In Psa 73:16 'thought' is to reflect and try to understand: the psalmist turns the matter over and finds it wearisome until he enters the sanctuary. Verses: Psa 73:16.
In Ecc 9:10 'thought' is the Hebrew noun for reckoning or account: the verse says there is no work, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Sheol. Verses: Ecc 9:10.
In 1Ch 28:9 'thought' is the Hebrew word for a plan or device that the Lord understands, with every heart searched; David tells Solomon to serve with a whole heart. Verses: 1Ch 28:9.
In 2Sa 3:19 'thought good' renders the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom 'in the eyes of': what seemed good to Israel and Benjamin. Verses: 2Sa 3:19.
In Jon 1:6 'give a thought' is the Hebrew verb of taking thought or caring: the captain hopes the god will think of them so they may not perish. Verses: Jon 1:6.
In Job 12:5 'thought' is the Hebrew noun for the settled thinking of the one at ease: it despises misfortune. The verse ties the thought to the circumstance of ease. Verses: Job 12:5.
In Mic 2:8 'with no thought of war' is the Hebrew verb of turning back from war: the trusting passers-by who are stripped have returned from fighting. Verses: Mic 2:8.

In Amo 4:13 'thought' is the Hebrew word for musing or meditation: God, the maker of mountains and wind, declares to man what his thought is; the verse does not say it is God's own thought. Verses: Amo 4:13.

older_inner_being.text: God also speaks in his heart.
Responsibility sits from lodging onward.
Intention: "every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen 6:5); "the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Gen 8:21).

Where it is placed. The verses place this in the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way"* (Pro 16:9); *"who plan evil things in their heart"* (Psa 140:2); *"the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1Ki 12:33); *"the purposes of the heart"* (1Co 4:5); *"every intention of the thoughts of his heart"* (Gen 6:5)
The Hebrew Bible: The source is the *lēv* (heart), not the brain. Examples are Proverbs 4:23 ("from it flow the springs of life") and Genesis 6:5 ("every intention of the thoughts of his heart").

1. From within: the heart is where they come from.: Mark 7:21 and Matthew 15:19 say it directly: "from within, out of the heart … come evil thoughts."; Genesis 6:5 speaks of "the intention of the thoughts of his heart," and Luke 1:51 of "the thoughts of their hearts."; Also Hebrews 4:12, Luke 2:35, 1 Chronicles 29:18, Matthew 9:4 and Luke 5:22.; In these verses thoughts are never located in the head. They come out of the heart, the centre of the person.

Where responsibility sits. The commands address the stages from lodging onward: "forsake … his thoughts" (Isa 55:7); "let none of you devise evil" (Zech 7:10); "take every thought captive" (2 Cor 10:5); "wash your heart" (Jer 4:14); The *arising* is not commanded, but it is not neutral either. What comes up shows the condition of the heart (Gen 6:5; Mark 7:21). So thoughts that arise reveal the heart, and devising engages the will. The heart itself can be changed from outside: written on, given discretion, guarded, or darkened.
Thought as reckoning, i.e.

What thoughts are: Design: forming something that does not yet exist. H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is what it is designed toward.; Reckoning: giving something its value or category. H2803H/J (60 rows): Human misreckoning: Eli "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Sam 1:13), "we esteemed him stricken" and "we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3–4), Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Gen 38:15).; God's reckoning: "he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Ps 32:2), and the nations "accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isa 40:15, 17).; To think is to judge the worth of something, and people can judge wrongly.; Inner speech.; "all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Ps 10:4). The thought is quoted as a sentence.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1 Sam 1:13).; *Dialogismos* covers both inner reasoning and outward "argument", "quarreling" and "disputing".; "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15).; Something that affects the body and emotions.; "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6; also 4:19; 5:10; 7:28).; "the cares of my heart" (Ps 94:19), and "haste within me" (Job 20:2).; A divided mind stalls a person: "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21, H5587A).; Creaturely and passing.; "but a breath" (Ps 94:11).; "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Ps 146:4).; "futile" (1 Cor 3:20; Rom 1:21).; "striving of heart … striving after wind" (Eccl 2:22; 4:16).
Thought as likening, i.e.
God thinks and plans, and his purpose stands over human plans

What the sight moves in a person, as the verses name it (G-person): "Was not my soul grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25); "He has pity on the weak and the needy" (Psa 72:13, the king); "you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand" (Deu 15:7); "an unworthy thought in your heart" (Deu 15:9); "Whoever mocks the poor … he who is glad at calamity" (Pro 17:5); "The poor is disliked even by his neighbor" (Pro 14:20); "All a poor man's brothers hate him" (Pro 19:7); "the poor man's wisdom is despised" (Ecc 9:16); "These are only the poor; they have no sense" (Jer 5:4); "no one remembered that poor man" (Ecc 9:15); "the very thing I was eager to do" (Gal 2:10); "pleased to make some contribution for the poor" (Rom 15:26); "not because he cared about the poor" (Joh 12:6); "the master of the house became angry and said … bring in the poor" (Luk 14:21).

Grudging heart / evil eye: "your heart shall not be grudging when you give" (Deu 15:10); "lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart … and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother" (Deu 15:9).

Hidden sin in the heart: "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" (Job 1:5); "You shall not hate your brother in your heart … lest you incur sin" (Lev 19:17); "an unworthy thought in your heart … and you be guilty of sin" (Deu 15:9)

5.1 Guarding one's own inner seat: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life" (Pro 4:23). Context 4:20–27 — the guarding moves outward: words kept "within your heart" (21) → "life … and healing to all their flesh" (22); keep the heart (23); → the mouth: "put away … crooked speech" (24); → the eyes: "look directly forward" (25); → the feet: "Ponder the path of your feet" (26–27); "take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget … lest they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9) — guarding the soul means guarding memory; "guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth" (Mal 2:15–16) [U+H1; H1]; "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34) → §7.6; "restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself" (Gal 6:1) [X]; "Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart" (Deu 15:9); "Take care lest your heart be deceived" (Deu 11:16); "Be very careful, therefore [*guard well your souls*], to love the Lord" (Jos 23:11) — distance 0: the "careful" word *is* the nephesh phrase

The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).
God knows the inclination before the act: 'I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land' (Deut 31:21); the Lord 'understands every plan' (1Chr 28:9).

The thoughts of people are open to God and to Jesus: God discerns, knows and understands them (Ps 139:2; 1Chr 28:9; Isa 66:18), Jesus perceives them (Luke 5:22; Matt 9:4), and the word of God discerns them (Heb 4:12); the speaker of Ps 139:23 asks God to know his thoughts.

Know and serve with the whole inner being. *"know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1Ch 28:9).

God sees the intention: *"the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1Ch 28:9).; *"the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth"* (Gen 8:21; also Gen 6:5).; *"he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust"* (Psa 103:14). H3336 here is "frame", the thing formed.; *"will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1Co 4:5).
The inclination can be kept, directed and stayed.
David asks God to keep his people's purposes: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1Ch 29:18).

How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.
Thought shaped by ease is contempt
Thought moves the body and emotions ("his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way"; "limping between two different opinions")
Flow 3: thoughts act back on the thinker.
Thought as inner speech, often quoted as a sentence

It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.
Thinking alone can stall; the sanctuary changes what it sees
God searching the anxious heart: "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts [anxious thoughts]" (Psa 139:23) [lexical].

1.4 God knows, tests and searches the heart: "you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1Ki 8:39; 2Ch 6:30); "he knows the secrets of the heart" (Psa 44:21); "God knows your hearts" (Luk 16:15); "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!" (Psa 139:23); "he who searches mind and heart" (Rev 2:23); "testing you to know what was in your heart" (Deu 8:2; 2Ch 32:31; Deu 13:3 "with all your heart and with all your soul")

8.1 God tests the heart: "I know, my God, that you test the heart" (1Ch 29:17); "I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (Jer 17:10); "the Lord tests hearts" — like crucible and furnace (Pro 17:3); "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!" (Psa 139:23); "Prove me, O Lord, and try me; test my heart and my mind" (Psa 26:2); "You have tried my heart … you will find nothing" (Psa 17:3); "you who test the minds and hearts" (Psa 7:9; Jer 11:20; 20:12); "you … test my heart toward you" (Jer 12:3); "God who tests our hearts" (1Th 2:4); "testing you to know what was in your heart" (Deu 8:2); "the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love … with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deu 13:3); "God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart" (2Ch 32:31)

(f) Anxiety handed over or answered.; "do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Phili 4:6) → "the peace of God … will guard your hearts and your minds" (4:7); "casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1Pe 5:7); "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psa 94:19); "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad" (Pro 12:25); "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts [*sar'appim*, anxious thoughts]" (Psa 139:23); The movement: anxiety is given to another, or answered by a word, and becomes peace or gladness. The seat is named where the anxiety sits (heart) and where the answer lands (soul, hearts and minds).

Seat. Anxiety holds the most in-verse seats of any M20 phenomenon (8 of 30). The seat word plays three different roles, and v3 separates them.; The seat as where the anxiety sits (bearer's own, genuine): Pro 12:25 "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 ("Anxiety in the heart").; Luk 21:34 "lest your hearts be weighed down with … cares of this life" (strand e). Batch A v3 §6.; Psa 139:23 "know my heart! … know my thoughts [anxious thoughts]" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 ("God searching the anxious heart").; The seat as where the answer lands (bearer's own, genuine): Psa 94:19 "your consolations cheer my soul" (strand f). Batch A v3 §6 notes that "heart" in this verse is English only. New in v3 [lexical]: the Hebrew locates the cares "within me" (*beqirbi*) and names the *nephesh* only at the receiving end. In Hebrew, the seat is named where the consolation arrives, not where the anxiety sits.; Phili 4:6 → 4:7 "will guard your hearts and your minds" (v1 §2 *merimnaō* row).; The seat as the object the anxiety is about (bearer's own, but not its location): Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22 "do not be anxious about your life [*psychē*] … nor about your body". Batch A v3 §6 ("Anxiety about life (psychē) and body"). New in v3, seat-sense: *psychē* here is the life that needs food. The next verse puts it so: "For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing" (Luk 12:23). The seat word is what the anxiety is about, not where it happens. The whole discourse inherits this frame (v1 §1.4: "discourse-level seat").; 1Cor 7:34 "anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit" (strand c). Batch A v3 §6 ("Divided interests") [H]. New in v3: here too the spirit is the object of the care, what she wants to be holy, and the care has a good aim. Within strand (c), the seat is on the undivided side of the divided care.; The seat as what dread displaces (the dreader's own, genuine): Isa 57:11 "did not lay it to heart". Batch D v2 §4.6 ("fear → lying → not laying to heart"). New in v3: the heart is not where the dread sits. It is the place God should have been set, and dread took that place instead.; Outside the verse, other seats in the strands:

Where they seem to agree (Claude's reading, worth testing).: Thought isn't simply self-authored.; Science: most processing is automatic and unconscious. Predictive-processing models describe the brain as constantly generating expectations before we are aware of them.; Philosophy: phenomenology observes that thoughts arrive rather than being made.; Bible: the heart runs deeper than we can see into. Jeremiah 17:9–10 says the heart is beyond knowing except by God, and in Psalm 139:23 the psalmist asks God to "know my thoughts."; Thought is shaped by what it takes in and dwells on.; Science: neuroplasticity. Repeated patterns strengthen connections.; Philosophy: Vygotsky's view that language and culture are internalised.; Bible: Proverbs 4:23 (guard the heart), Romans 12:2 (be transformed by the renewing of the mind) and Philippians 4:8 (think on these things).

12 (new) | Whether thought is brought to God | Emerging | Cares met by consolation (Psa 94:19); thoughts offered for searching (139:23); thinking that stalls until the sanctuary (73:17); thoughts captive to obey Christ (2Co 10:5)
Multiplying thoughts, toward us: "your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you" (Psa 40:5).
Thought is creaturely and passing

5. God is a thinker too, and his thinking has the last word. The same vocabulary is used of God: *maḥăšāvāh*: Jer 29:11; Ps 33:11; 40:5; 92:5; Isa 55:8–9; *ḥāšav*: Jer 18:11; 2 Sam 14:14; Lam 2:8; "the Lord takes thought for me" (Ps 40:17); "that you think of him" (Ps 144:3); *mᵊzimmāh*: "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20); "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2); In Gen 50:20 there are two opposite intentions about one event, expressed with the same verb: "you meant evil … God meant it for good." Human plans are real, but "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21; also Prov 16:9; Ps 33:10–11; Job 5:12).
False likeness: God likened to man ("you thought that I was one like yourself"); man likened to God ("I will make myself like the Most High"; "I am a god"; "you consider yourself a lion").

Poor or needy said by the speaker as the ground of a plea: "answer me, for I am poor and needy" (Psa 86:1); "I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God!" (Psa 70:5); "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psa 40:17).

1.6 Plans for welfare, and thought for the one in need: *"For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope"* (Jer 29:11).; The verse looks ahead to *"When seventy years are completed"* (29:10).; It is followed by *"You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart"* (29:13).; *"As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me"* (Psa 40:17).; *"But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (2Sa 14:14). The wise woman says it against the fact that *"We must all die"*.
The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet"; meditate day and night "so that you may be careful to do"

9.3 From thought to action (Claude's reading): The verses trace a path from thought to deed: Arising. Thoughts come, often in the night (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Ezek 38:10; Luke 24:38).; Lodging. They stay and are dwelt on (Jer 4:14).; Reckoning. They weigh up and value things (Isa 53:4; 1 Sam 1:13).; Devising. They take the form of a plan (Ezek 38:10b; Ps 36:4).; Expression. Tongue, lips and eyes: "your tongue plots" (Ps 52:2), "devise words of deceit" (Ps 35:20), "winks his eyes plans" (Prov 16:30), "whisper … imagine the worst" (Ps 41:7).; Action. Hand and feet: "when the morning dawns, they perform it" (Mic 2:1); "a heart that devises … feet that make haste" (Prov 6:18); "their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isa 59:7).; The same path also runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).

The relation between God's thinking and human thinking runs both ways. God reckons (Gen 15:6; Ps 32:2) and overrules: "you meant evil … God meant it for good" (Gen 50:20); "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21). Human thought can also turn back toward God: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).
Pure words against impure thoughts: "The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord, but gracious words are pure" (Pro 15:26).
Thoughts to be forsaken: "let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isa 55:7). The next line gives the answer: "for he will abundantly pardon".
The path: arising → lodging → reckoning → devising → expression (tongue, lips, eyes) → action (hand, feet)

Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations": The Lord sees beneath the choosing: *"For I know their works and their thoughts"* (v18).; The tremblers are promised the opposite outcome: *"You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice"* (v14).
The heart is where thoughts come from

Where it comes from: the agent's own heart: Assyria: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; for he says: 'Are not my commanders all kings?'" (Isa 10:7–8); Babylon: "I was angry with my people … I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end" (47:6–7). And "who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me'" (47:8).
(v2) Isa 10:5 (UA): Context seat: Isa 10:7 "his heart does not so think … in his heart to destroy"; Whose · check: Assyria's · genuine; Already read in: F v4 §12.1; C v3 §2.1; §: §37.

12.1 The heart's own purpose inside God's purpose: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few" (Isa 10:7); [Claude reading] Assyria is the Lord's rod (Isa 10:5), but its heart has its own intention. The instrument's heart does not share the purpose of the one who wields it. This underlies the judgment on the instrument that follows (10:12 — Batch D §9.1, "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria").

Evil devised in the heart: "who plan evil things in their heart" (Psa 140:2); "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10; 8:17); "thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme" (Eze 38:10); "his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isa 10:7)

3.1 It happens in the heart, and it is hidden until it acts: *"Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass"* (Pro 16:30). The planning shows only in small signs.; *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jer 11:19). Jeremiah did not see the plan aimed at him.; *"they intended to do me harm"* (Neh 6:2). The intent sat behind the friendly invitation, *"Come and let us meet together"*.; *"But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy"* (Isa 10:7). Of Assyria, what is in the heart differs from the role God gives it. I read this as the intention belonging to the one who holds it, whatever use another makes of the act.; *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme"* (Eze 38:10). Here the thought arrives first and the devising follows. This is the one verse in the set that states such a sequence; no other verse is joined to it here.; *"you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Neh 6:8). The same capacity can produce what is false.

1. The heart or mind is the place thoughts come from. Mark 7:21 and Matt 15:19 ("out of the heart come evil thoughts"). Also: "a heart that devises wicked plans" (Prov 6:18); "plan evil things in their heart" (Ps 140:2); "devise evil … in your heart" (Zech 7:10; 8:17); "The heart of man plans his way" (Prov 16:9); "his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isa 10:7); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luke 9:47); In Jer 4:14, thoughts *lodge* within: "How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?" This follows the call to "wash your heart."
Thoughts lodge and stay

The verses: Daniel: *"it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth"* (4:22).; *"your kingdom shall be confirmed for you from the time that you know that Heaven rules"* (4:26).; Daniel's counsel: *"break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed"* (4:27).; Twelve months later: *"Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"* (4:30).; *"While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven"* (4:31).; Before giving the interpretation, Daniel *"was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him"*, and he wishes the dream on the king's enemies (4:19).
Night thoughts: revelation when God makes them known; alarm without that; a claimed night vision can be wrong
Thoughts arise unbidden, often at night, and can be tied to revelation

2. Not by comparing. "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor" (Gal 6:3–4). Thinking oneself something when one is nothing is named self-deception.
